items.title: Why smart people stay stuck in research mode
items.summary: I recently had coffee with a university colleague who told me she was in the middle of planning a workshop. She had bought a couple of books about hosting workshops, had created a spreadsheet projecting attendance under different scenarios, and was now comparing ticketing platforms. But she still hadn’t invited a single person. We talked about how none of that research was necessarily a waste of time. When you love learning, figuring out the best approach can be enjoyable in itself. But every answer can produce another question, and before you know it, preparation has become the project. Worse, that endless research keeps you busy while the harder questions wait: Will anybody be interested? Am I any good at this? The psychology of endless research You could call this a problem of overthinking, but research points instead to several nuanced and overlapping tendencies that can make gathering information feel easier, safer, and more satisfying than taking action. A better option could be hiding somewhere. You might find a venue that suits your workshop and still spend another weekend looking because there might be an even better option out there. Psychologists call this tendency to seek the best possible choice maximizing , and studies suggest that people higher in maximizing tendency explore more alternatives before selecting one. Research feels like a respectable form of avoidance. The task we’re avoiding may expose us to rejection, uncertainty, or embarrassment; reading about it does not. In that way, psychologists have argued that procrastination can serve as a form of short-term mood regulation, which is why we often find ourselves opening another tab instead of taking action. Thinking itself can feel rewarding. Psychologists use the term need for cognition to describe how much people enjoy sustained mental effort. People higher in this trait tend to put more effort into decisions and are less inclined to change their research approach under time pressure. Without a clear sense of when to stop, it’s easy to keep looking. Researchers found that participants with a stronger need for certainty spend longer gathering information, particularly when there is no clear rule for making a choice. You might have studied many different ways to run workshops, without knowing what would make one preferable to the others. Reading more about each approach may give you a better understanding of your options without bringing you any closer to a decision. Taken together, these tendencies help explain why the research phase of a project can be so tempting to linger in. Depending on your intellectual curiosity and how you respond to uncertainty, mapping possibilities and comparing approaches can feel more rewarding than the practical work of bringing an idea to life. This isn’t limited to professional projects — the same pattern can show up when you’re exploring a new hobby or trying to change a habit. You can spend weeks learning about something without ever taking action to find out what it’s like to actually do it. How to turn research into action If you tend to get stuck in research mode, you don’t need to force yourself to become less curious. You just need to recognize when you’ve learned enough theory, and when your question can only be answered through direct experience. Here are three simple steps you can follow to put what you’ve learned into practice and use the results to decide what to do next: 1. First, take stock of what you know. Write down what you’ve already learned about the different moving parts of the project. Alongside it, list the concrete ideas you could act on. You’ll probably find that your bottleneck isn’t more theoretical knowledge, but evidence and direct experience from the real world. 2. Next, run a tiny experiment. Decide what you will test and the trial period, using this mini protocol: I will [action] for [duration]. For the would-be workshop organizer, this could be: “I will invite three people to a 30-minute pilot session each week for three weeks.” The point isn’t to figure out every single detail, but to collect the real-world data no comparison chart can ever tell you: whether people show up, the questions they ask, and what parts you enjoy running. 3. Finally, reflect before deciding on your next steps. What surprised you? What would you change? Use those observations to design another tiny experiment or — if you do need to conduct more research — to explore a more focused question with a clear stopping rule for making a choice. Good research helps us make better decisions, but there are questions it simply cannot answer without real-world data. By applying an experimental mindset , you can gather evidence about what works, what doesn’t, and what you still need to figure out. You may still have plenty of questions after your first experiment. Some might send you back to your research, this time with a clearer idea of what you’re looking for. Others may turn out to be far less important than you imagined. The only way to find out is to try something and see what actually happens. And in the meantime, you’ll have made some progress on bringing your idea to life. This article Why smart people stay stuck in research mode is featured on Big Think .

items.title: An Adaptation That’s Both ‘Excellent’ and ‘Bizarre’
items.summary: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. Somewhere in the back of my closet sits a strange relic: a virtual-reality viewer made of cardboard. The only thing I remember watching on it, in 2017, was a 10-minute adaptation of George Saunders’s Booker Prize–winning debut novel, Lincoln in the Bardo . Produced by The New York Times , this 3-D, 360-degree experience was effectively a staged excerpt of the book—which features Abraham Lincoln, his freshly dead 11-year-old son, and a chorus of grotesque ghosts—that could be viewed in full only by constantly swiveling one’s head. Google Cardboard, as this tech was known, was discontinued long ago; a decade later, the most notable thing about this experiment is that it was not the first or the last unconventional incarnation of Saunders’s highly unconventional novel. This week, the Atlantic senior editor Talya Zax admired the boldness of the book’s latest adaptation , an “excellent” and “bizarre” staging at New York’s Metropolitan Opera. Her essay inspired me to dip into the Bardo audiobook, which is memorable for being packed with 166 narrators, many of them celebrities . Spoiler: It holds up. First, here are six new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: The rise of the sexy-cozy autumn read Celebrity has become a jobs program. The Greek island that taught me the art of living “Peeling the Orange,” a poem by Howard Altmann Democrats are sounding more like Republicans. How the American Girl doll lost its way Zax argues that Bardo benefits from opera’s “freedom to be outlandish,” and that a film version would have to contend instead with Hollywood’s “risk-averse studio system.” The book is surreal, full of overlapping dialogue, madcap characters, and descriptions that defy any visual logic. This much is immediately clear, however: Willie Lincoln, the president’s deceased son, is in a sort of graveyard purgatory, which he must escape before it destroys him. Helping him are three oddly contorted ghosts—a mysteriously damned reverend, a priapic printmaker who never consummated his marriage, and a gay man who died by suicide. Telling the story of Lincoln’s grief at the height of the Civil War, Saunders alternates between snippets from the historical record and the cemetery’s giant cast of specters. This is certainly the stuff of opera. It is also fodder for an audiobook that rises above its stunt casting. The recording’s collection of notables resembles the slate of an animated Disney movie motivated by star power: Susan Sarandon, Julianne Moore, Ben Stiller, Don Cheadle, Bill Hader, Lena Dunham, Carrie Brownstein, and Keegan-Michael Key all voice characters. The A-listers get the plum roles, of course, and many of them do effectively dramatize the material; Dunham’s teenage girl is affectingly tormented, Key’s enslaved shade righteously wrathful, Hader’s low-class brawler fabulously profane. The documentary snippets are less effective, voiced largely by colleagues and friends, including 60 employees of Saunders’s publisher, Penguin Random House. Then again, this may have as much to do with the doldrums in those segments of the book as the talent of the cast. The standout performances, however, are from Nick Offerman, David Sedaris, and Saunders himself as Willie’s three helpful ghosts. They have the best material, including sections in which they inhabit the (technically nonspeaking) president’s thoughts. And they showcase what’s best about any effective audiobook. It’s a dramatic rendering, to a degree, but it preserves the interiority and verbal dexterity that only a novel can hold. The banter among this trio is crisp, funny, and layered with meaning, and the soliloquies reminded me that this is Saunders at the height of his power, balancing satire and pathos better than almost any writer I can think of. This eccentric recording is mainstream in one important way: It delivers on its promise of rendering the book faithfully and with a generous dose of flair. Karen Almond / Met Opera The Best Kind of Book Adaptation By Talya Zax A new opera based on George Saunders’s novel Lincoln in the Bardo makes some fantastically shocking choices. Read the full article. What to Read Beloved , by Toni Morrison Beloved asks readers to imagine something as pure and perfect as love—a mother caring for her child; two broken people trying to make something beautiful—in the face of absolute misery and ugliness. That’s where the book’s potency comes from: the tension between the darkness and the light. Sethe, its main character, has committed unspeakable violence toward her own daughter, but she was motivated by maternal devotion. Having survived that transformational tragedy, she has to decide whether she can allow anyone to love her again. Beloved evokes both the peril of motherhood and its singular power. Reading it, I wanted to fold myself into the pages and then fall out of my skin. It’s painful, but what’s even more devastating is that the novel is one of the most banned books in America. How dare we rob the next generation of its greatness? — Jenisha Watts From our list: 50 unforgettable love stories Out Next Week 📚 How to Be Less Useful , by Priyanka Mattoo 📚 West of Loveland , by Tom Drury 📚 The Channel , by Jana Prikryl Your Weekend Read Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic. Source: Getty. Why Are Political Candidates Emailing Like Ex-Boyfriends and Car Salesmen? By Sophie Haigney The text, sent from an unknown number, prompted a jump scare when I saw it as an iMessage preview: “About last night …” The night before: Hadn’t I been at yoga? When I clicked on the message, I was relieved and then annoyed by the next words: “—Jon Ossoff,” under an image of the senator from Georgia staring into the middle distance, handsomely. “Last night I took the stage to debate my MAGA extremist opponent Mike Collins,” “Ossoff” went on to tell me. The text message continued over the course of several paragraphs and ended, as these missives tend to, with an ask for cash. Read the full article. items.title: Forget Grit
items.summary: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. In retrospect , 2016, the year that Angela Duckworth published Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance , may have been a high-water mark for the dogged go-getter‑ism she was selling. Her book landed just as Hillary Clinton, that avatar of tenacity, seemed poised to win the presidency and Alexander Hamilton was rapping on Broadway about not giving up his shot. You could still just barely discern within each of the billionaires who bestrode Silicon Valley the dork with unusual willpower who had made it. And among the books clustered near Grit in airport bookstores—where the American self is apparently at its most moldable—were other pitches for individual hardiness, including efforts to make Stoicism hot again. When I read Grit now, it feels to me like a taunt. Economic mobility has stalled, nonhumans are encroaching on our jobs, and COVID has scarred us with the knowledge that the unforeseen can creep up at any moment. You can be as gritty as sandpaper and still feel trampled on. Duckworth herself now seems ready to concede that our mind alone can’t control the direction of our life, that it doesn’t all happen “from the inside out,” as she put it in Grit . Back then, she arrived at the not-quite-mind-blowing conclusion that to be “the best of the best”—as accomplished as Olympic swimmers, Scripps National Spelling Bee champions, the president of Cinnabon—you had to really care about winning and work hard at it. “Today I wake up every day asking the same question that led me to psychology in the first place: Why are some people more successful than others? ” she writes in her new book, Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best . “But I no longer believe that a complete answer begins and ends with the individual.” Adam Grant, another best-selling psychologist, appears to have hit a similar wall. In Vibe: The Secrets of Strong Connections in a Lonely World , his sixth book, he departs from his relentless focus on self-transformation and looks instead at “the quality of connection between people.” For an author whose previous books are mostly about remaking yourself in the image of superachievers (he, too, has a thing for elite swimmers), this new endeavor feels like a departure: to consider that mercurial thing that happens between us and other people. Duckworth and Grant are colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania (he is at the Wharton School). They are also both associated with positive psychology, the field created by Martin Seligman at the school in the late 1990s—Seligman was Duckworth’s dissertation adviser. He rejected psychology’s focus on mental illness and wanted to identify the conditions under which human “flourishing” happens. Positive psychology was, at least in its own self-understanding, trying to apply empirical science to the ancient philosophical question of how to live a good life; Seligman wanted, as he recently wrote , to see if the field could “make the world a better place.” But the approach underwent something of a corporate transformation as it migrated into business schools and HR departments. One of Duckworth’s first grit studies examined the kind of cadet who thrives at West Point , and Grant looked at businesses such as Google and Facebook. Their evidence base, case studies, and examples continued to be drawn overwhelmingly from schools, companies, elite performers, and athletes (all those swimmers). What they were measuring was how you maximize performance, which is some distance from Aristotle. By the time the psychologists each strapped on a microphone and took to the TED stage in the 2010s with compressed, bullet-point versions of their research, they were ready for the self-help-book section. Their arrival helped give a glow-up to an enterprise that has thrived from the start on the notion that your inner resources alone, properly unearthed and deployed, will propel you to become the most successful version of you. In Self-Help (1859), the book that gave the genre its name, the Scottish journalist Samuel Smiles wrote that “help from without is often enfeebling in its effects, but help from within invariably invigorates.” What method did advice-givers deploy? Extract formulas for inner drive from vivid models of extraordinary achievement, and never mind how much gets left out—those pesky forces of genetics and upbringing, economics and history, not to mention luck. Duckworth and Grant joined in, and their best sellers got blurbed by the business and media elite (Mark Cuban, Oprah Winfrey, Sheryl Sandberg, Arianna Huffington). Yet now they seem to be swerving onto more unruly terrain. Are their new books, I wondered, prepared to question some of the tenets of the venerable self-made-man myth? A person’s social world, the one outside their control that impinges on them at every turn, would seem to be key to understanding a rise or fall. Is that what Situated and Vibe , products of a disorienting moment, would do: look around and realize how little power we actually have over the course of our own lives? That isn’t what these books do. Grant does acknowledge the “uncertainty, complexity, and conflict” that characterize most of our encounters once we leave the confines of our mind. “Like it or not,” Duckworth now pauses to observe, “our every thought and action is profoundly shaped by our peers and mentors, by our culture, and even by the objects in our personal space.” Entire centuries-old fields of social science, as the authors both know well, have detailed how such forces influence us. But recognizing constraint and limitation is not what this genre is about. Its goal is to reassure us that we have ultimate control over our fate. Grant’s focus is on vibing, a word he uses to describe that ephemeral state when people or a group connect deeply—when “conversations pulse with energy. Thoughts soar. Trust grows. Time flies.” He insists that this is a “skill set that can be learned and taught,” and that it is crucial to one’s success. What follows is an assortment of studies to establish the ideal conditions for generating this crucial synergistic energy. In one of them , the same woman approached two different groups of male hikers trekking through a rainforest and, after asking them to fill out a questionnaire, she tore off a piece of paper, wrote down her number, and handed it to each of them. She met the first group on an ordinary bridge, and only one in eight men later called. But half of the men in the second group, which she encountered on a narrow suspension bridge swaying 230 feet above churning rapids, called her. The takeaway? What deepens a relationship is being in an “emotionally intense situation.” Again and again, Grant plucks broad lessons from social-psychology experiments so odd that I came away wondering how big the sample size could possibly be, whether correlation and causation were getting confused—and, not least, how to apply the findings. Grant proposes engineering a group outing to such a bridge or a haunted house or, God help me, an improv-comedy class. Unlike his earlier books, which are largely about shifting one’s mindset, there is only so much you can do to master your environment or other people, though Grant makes lots of suggestions. Throw dinner parties, but ensure that they are “carefully choreographed.” For example, ask guests to each throw one shoe in a pile and then take turns grabbing a shoe and holding it up for the owner to claim. “At dessert time, I prompted people to play musical chairs,” he proudly reports. I guess trust grew during these pre-K games? Often Grant slips into a style that reads like a manual for robots learning how to act like humans. “Laughing during and after disagreements,” he advises, “is one of the most effective ways to maintain a healthy bond.” But you can’t really reverse engineer something like vulnerability or attentiveness or love. items.title: Our Favorite Short Stories, Flash Fiction, and Poetry to Read for Halloween
items.summary: As soon as the sticky summer air begins to dissipate and the first leaves transition into fiery reds and oranges, my instant desire is to cozy up with all things eerie and haunted. The winter holidays full of family, food, and chaos are imminent, but in this moment, I crave the youthful nostalgia of Halloween stories. While many of us turn to films and TV for jump scares or trick-or-treaters creeping in the shadows, don’t overlook the suspense that awaits through a written tale—like a hand slowly reaching out beneath the lines or a set of dark beady eyes watching you from the corners of the page. This Halloween, get lost in these stories and poems of dark woods, family histories, and lovers long gone from the archives of Recommended Reading and The Commuter . In these tales, language gives way to imagination. Some prose uncanny, some more sinister, others eerie pleasures. Let these stories carry you into the dark nights of winter’s approach. Grab an extra blanket and light the fire to ease the chill in your bones. Or let it creep up your spine and bask in the thrill just a little longer as Halloween inches closer. We have something for all to enjoy. “Good Night, Sleep Tight” by Brian Evenson “Good Night, Sleep Tight” is the perfect eerie and mysterious bedtime story for those unafraid of the monsters who live under the bed or hide in the closet. Sometimes the unsettling and uncanny is right beside us, in the people we trust to tuck us in for the night. In this short story, Brian Evenson’s narrator recounts the cozy bedtime stories his mother told him as a child. Yet, every now and then she’d return to his bedroom with a frightening one. Now as he, his wife, and son plan for a visit to his old childhood home to spend the weekend with his mother, he can’t help but worry those scary stories might be passed onto his own child. He’s forced to confront the truths and tales he’s long ignored from his childhood. “The Dirty Kid” by Mariana Enriquez Mariana Enriquez is known for her Latin American Gothic and horror short stories, so it’s no surprise that what might seem like a tale of crime in “The Dirty Kid” is far beyond a typical missing child. The story opens with a childhood home taken over by age and wear, pulling the reader into the perfect setting for a spooky tale. The neighborhood adds to the eeriness, as it was once inhabited by the Argentinian aristocrats who, centuries ago, fled the yellow fever epidemic, leaving their mansions empty. The large mansions decorated with gargoyles and ornate details rose up across the now desolate neighborhood. The neighborhood is overcome with rotting homes, faltering businesses, thieves and the unhoused. The narrator does not wish to abandon her family home, but when the homeless woman and child who live outside her door go missing, she begins to wonder if supernatural forces might be at play. “Tiptoe” by Laird Barron There is just something perfectly creepy about stories that follow adult characters returning to events from their childhood, especially when they’re left wondering if the people they’ve always known and loved are as they appear. In “Tiptoe” Laird Barron disarmingly exposes the animalistic nature which manifests within human desires. We’re taken back to a multifamily camping trip as the narrator searches for answers for a condition he’s experiencing, certain his wholesome childhood hasn’t left him with any traumas. The fright in this short story isn’t around the campfire, but instead resides deep in the woods and tiptoes ever so slowly to the reader. “King of All Hogs” by JG Lynas The middle of nowhere, an isolated farm house occupied by an older couple, a decrepit barn, a phone that keeps ringing—the ultimate formula of horror. In the short story “King of All Hogs,” the narrator and her boyfriend, Mark, seek out a small pig farm that Mark discovered on an online forum. From the start, the reader senses that the relationship itself is strange: built on an unsteady infatuation. Things only get weirder and more layered once they arrive at the farm and invite themselves to stay for dinner. What’s hiding in the barn? Are any characters trustworthy? Who’s on the other end of the phone? “Hannah-Beast” by Jennifer McMahon It’s Halloween night, kids are in costumes, homes are decorated with jack-o-lanterns and ghoulish delights. Thirteen-year-old Erin is all dressed and ready to go trick-or-treating with her friends when her mom, Amanda, scolds her for her costume, the Hannah-beast: thick blue face paint, a colorful clown wig, a silver cape. Erin doesn’t care that Hannah-beast was once worn by a local girl with a story that haunts their town, that’s part of the thrill. She’s resentful of her mother’s rules, unaware that Amanda’s overbearingness is more than parental concern. Jennifer McMahon shows readers how horrors of the past surface as she weaves through time in “Hannah-Beast.” “The Bone Friend” by Zebbie Watson In this flash fiction, Zebbie Watson spins a tale of the dead full of whimsy and longing. When a teenage girl unearths a body of bones, she decides to date him. The story is told through the point of view of the skeleton as he tries to fit into this new world but wonders about his history and who he was before he became an array of decayed bones. The story unfolds in beautiful poetic prose that leaves a melancholy ache in the reader. “Fucking Ghosts!” by Hannah Gregory Sometimes Halloween stories offer us ghostly themes and spectral backdrops overtaken by love or humor. In the flash piece, “Fucking Ghosts!” we get an ominous tale that morphs into something more quirky and fun. Hannah Gregory gives us a narrator that can’t shake her old lover who still visits her every October, and she finds herself masturbating in bar bathrooms anytime she feels a cold draft down her neck. She keeps her haunting sex life a secret from everyone until she meets someone who understands the heartache of losing a partner and going back to them even after they’re dead. “The Bone Hermit” by Lyndsey Croal “The Bone Hermit” is a haunting piece of flash fiction that leaves a lingering chill. It raises a creepy crawling feeling as a hermit crab inhabits the bones of the narrator’s deceased husband. While she thought she tucked the body safely away in a cove off the shore, the crab makes a home in the carcass and pieces of his body begin to show up outside her window, the crab peeking through the skull’s hollowed eyes. “I Pray in Screamers House of Horrors” by Domenica Martinello Which Book Should You Read This Halloween? Looking for haunted houses? Dark fairytales? Ghost stories? We've got your next read covered! --> Looking for haunted houses? Dark fairytales? Ghost stories? We’ve got your next read covered! Oct 25 – Electric Literature Reading Lists “I Pray in the Screamers House of Horrors” is the first poem in a set of poems by Domenica Martinello, where hope is born in a house of horrors. The poignant and visceral language captures scenes of addiction and healing from the narrator’s life, and makes the reader feel trapped, choking, searching for an escape, leaving one wondering if the light at the end of the tunnel is an illusion of warmth or more gnawing terror. The post Our Favorite Short Stories, Flash Fiction, and Poetry to Read for Halloween appeared first on Electric Literature .

items.title: 8 Novels About Spending Half Your Life at Work
items.summary: If you work 40 hours a week, you spend about a third of your waking hours at work. When you add the time you spend commuting to work, complaining about work, and stressing about work, you’re looking at half of your conscious life spent in the workplace. I’m fascinated by how much of our lives we spend working—and how rarely we get into the details. How many of your friends could describe how you spend your typical workday? We act as though work is boring, and yet, at every job I’ve ever held, my workday has been filled with tiny bursts of drama, ferocious irritations, minor victories, and long-standing power struggles. In my debut novel To Stay, To Stay, To Stay , I wanted to capture what the workday feels like minute by minute. What is it like to stand behind the counter of a bakery for eight hours, exchanging hundreds of pleasant greetings? What is it like to sit through a therapy appointment with client after client, assuring them all that they’re making progress? The novel’s omniscient narrator follows an ensemble cast through small-town life in Appalachian Ohio, from home to work to the places in between, as the characters wrestle with the vocations they’ve given half their lives to—all while wondering whether they’ve made the right choice. I love writers who can bring an unfamiliar workplace to life. In these eight novels, the daily grind is presented in obsessive, sometimes absurdist detail, turning the familiar into something uncanny and worth studying. There’s No Such Thing as an Easy Job by Kikuko Tsumura, translated by Polly Barton After a case of severe burnout at her last job, the unnamed protagonist of this novel tells an employment agency that she wants to find an easy job with very little drama and a lot of sitting. Luckily, such a job exists: monitoring live video surveillance of a reclusive writer, who is suspected to have hidden contraband in his office. But the protagonist quickly discovers that this seemingly mindless job comes with its own strange drawbacks—as do all the jobs she tries next. From a luxury cracker company to a hut in the forest, from writing bus ads to hanging up posters, the protagonist can’t seem to stay detached from the outsized enthusiasm, obsession, and vigor that possesses her coworkers. “I didn’t want to have any more feelings about my work than were strictly necessary,” she laments. But in the modern workplace, emotional labor is an unspoken part of the job description. The daily grind in this novel is absurd as well as intimately recognizable, and weirdly engrossing. It’s hard not to care about work, it turns out, even when you’re reading about someone else’s. The New Me by Halle Butler Millie is as stuck as a failed-to-launch millennial can get. She has a good education, but has ended up in a series of dispiriting temp jobs. Her parents help pay for her apartment, while Millie can barely bring herself to cook or clean. She hates everyone, but she’s also lonely. She puts people off with her lack of effort, but when she makes an effort, that puts people off too. The only way out that Millie can see is the glimmer of a full-time job offer—but as she devotes herself to secretarial work, the reader catches on that even this slight hope is not what it seems. The New Me is relentless in its exposure of the hollowness of workplace culture, and of the void where any alternative fulfillment would go. Superfan by Jenny Tinghui Zhang It may seem that performing on stage to thousands of adoring fans is an ideal job. And yet, in Superfan , Jenny Tinghui Zhang captures the daily grind of a beloved boy band: hours of choreography, eating and sleeping on a schedule, getting shunted from cars to hotel rooms and back into cars, coached before every interview. Even in their free time, the boy band is beholden to their fans, posting seemingly candid videos to social media, and stoking their fans’ feeling of personal connection. This novel will not make you want to join a boy band—on the contrary, it shows how much labor goes into forming and maintaining a parasocial relationship from both ends. The boys in the band must continually hawk their stage personas through bite-sized bits of media, and the fans must comb through all the footage and interviews and performances to catch some glimpse of the real people inside those personas. It’s a ton of work on both sides, and the reward of all that work is that you get to do more of it. Severance by Ling Ma On its surface, Severance is a pandemic novel—but it is most precise and haunting in its critique of our relationship to work. Candace Chen works at a book publisher, where she coordinates the printing of expensive custom bibles and envies her much cooler colleagues, the Art Girls. As the mysterious Shen Flu virus begins to shut down businesses around the world, the protagonist accepts a lucrative offer: She’ll keep coming into the New York office for another year, in exchange for a hefty severance package. Even as the world ends, she is sending follow-up emails, tolerating the two-hour, then three-hour, then four-hour commute into work, and wandering the silent streets of Manhattan. Until one day she locks herself out of the office and it hits her: The city around her is empty, and she is the only one left. Severance captures the curious inertia of the salaried job, especially those jobs where the work is meaningless enough to justify leaving, but the money is good enough to justify staying. Stoner by John Williams William Stoner gives himself entirely to the work of loving and teaching literature. In so doing, he alienates students, battles with colleagues, dooms his marriage, and dies unremembered. It is impossible to read the account of the small victories and painful setbacks of Stoner’s life without both rooting for him and resigning oneself to his eventual disappointment. This novel maps out the long and embattled path of academia, from youthful ambition to cutthroat office politics to the fading of relevance. Through it all, Stoner somehow continues to love teaching, and to value the opportunity he has to discuss literature with successive generations of students. Stoner is a compassionate and unsparing view of the life of professors, and shows how even this apparently cushy daily grind has its share of hard and thankless labor. The Adjunct by Maria Adelmann For a fresh take on the grind of academia, try Maria Adelmann’s new novel The Adjunct . The protagonist, Sam, is an overworked and underpaid adjunct professor, frantically seeking to make ends meet as the ghosts of her past crop up and complicate things. The professor she once had a not-quite-affair with has written a book that everyone thinks is about her, and meanwhile she’s got to stay on top of five classes and eventually somehow pay off her credit card bill. Written in unsparing, furious detail, The Adjunct is a deep and perilous dive into the plight of the modern adjunct, from side hustles, to parking fees, to late nights grading, to the dangled carrot of a real, stable, full-time job. As the owner of the shop gradually comes to trust and then depend on Frank, it seems that the shop may be saved from irrelevance and eventual bankruptcy.
